title: Does Bleach Kill Mold? Only on Hard, Non-Porous Surfaces
description: Yes, but only on hard surfaces: bleach kills mold on tile, glass and tubs, yet on wood and drywall it mostly whitens the stain. Use RMR-141 and fix the damp.
dek: Bleach kills mold on tile, glass and tubs, but on wood and drywall it mostly whitens the stain.
intro: On hard, non-porous surfaces, yes. On wood, drywall and anything that soaks up water, it mostly erases the stain and leaves the problem in place. Here is the surface-by-surface answer.

Bleach kills mold on surfaces that mold cannot get into: glazed tile, glass, a fiberglass tub. On wood, drywall and other porous materials it whitens the stain on top while the growth inside the material carries on, which is exactly why it looks like it worked. The EPA does not recommend bleach as a routine part of mold cleanup. Use it in the shower, and use something else everywhere else.

quickAnswer: Does bleach kill mold? Chlorine bleach is a strong oxidiser, and when it reaches mold on a smooth, sealed surface it kills it. That is not in dispute, and it is why bathroom sprays built on sodium hypochlorite, such as Clorox Plus Tilex Mold & Mildew Remover, carry a kill claim on the label. Clorox says the product kills 99.9 percent of mold and mildew, and on glazed tile, glass and fiberglass that is a fair description of what happens.

sections.h: Does Bleach Kill Mold? at a Glance

blocks.p: The trouble is that most mold in a house is not growing on glazed tile. It is on the back of drywall, in the grain of a joist, along a wooden window sill, in the paper of a basement wall or deep in an old grout line. Those materials are porous. Mold sends its root-like filaments, called hyphae, into them, and a liquid sprayed on the face of the material does not reliably follow. What bleach does very well on those surfaces is remove colour, so the dark patch fades and the job looks done.

That is the heart of the bleach question. Bleach removes the stain, and the stain is the only part of the mold most people can see. When the black spots vanish in thirty seconds it is natural to assume the mold is dead, but the visible stain and the living colony are not the same thing. If the colony is inside the material and the moisture that fed it is still there, it comes back, often in the same outline, within weeks.

So the honest answer has three parts. Yes, bleach kills mold on hard, non-porous surfaces, and it is a reasonable choice for shower grout, tile and tubs. No, it is not a dependable mold killer for wood, drywall, ceiling tiles, carpet or concrete, and its own makers say not to use it on several of those. And whatever you use, the EPA's guidance is that the real job is removing the mold and fixing the moisture, not sterilising the surface.
THE RULE
Bleach for tile, glass and tubs. Not for wood, drywall or anything that soaks up water.
If water soaks into it, bleach will not reach the mold inside it. Use a registered non-bleach fungicide there, and fix the moisture source either way.

Bleach earns its reputation in the bathroom. Shower mildew grows on the surface of glazed ceramic tile, glass doors, acrylic and fiberglass surrounds and the silicone at the edge of the tub. None of those materials lets the mold get inside, so the whole colony is exposed to whatever you spray on it. A bleach-based spray reaches all of it, kills it and removes the black pigment in one step, which is why a dirty shower can look new in a minute.

Clorox is unusually specific about where its Tilex spray belongs. The product page lists grout, glazed ceramic tile, tubs, fiberglass, glass shower doors, vinyl shower curtains, counters, sinks and no-wax floors. It also lists where not to use it: wood, painted surfaces, aluminium, fabric, carpet and paper, and it says to rinse it promptly off rubber, plastic and vinyl. That list is the best summary of the bleach question you will find, and it comes from the company that sells the bleach.

Grout sits in the middle. Sealed, sound grout in a regularly cleaned shower behaves much like tile, and surface mildew on it responds well to a bleach spray. Old, unsealed or crumbling grout is more porous, and black spots that keep returning in the same place within a week or two of cleaning usually mean the growth is deeper than a spray can reach. At that point the fix is to rake out and regrout, or at least reseal once it is clean and dry, rather than reaching for a stronger bottle.

Will bleach kill black mold? Black mold is a description, not a species. Plenty of common household molds are dark green or black, and colour does not change how a product works on them. On a non-porous surface, bleach kills dark mold the same way it kills any other. On a porous one, it bleaches the dark colour out of the surface and leaves the colony underneath. The surface decides the answer, not the colour of the spots, and that is true whether the label says black mold, mildew or anything else.

One practical note from the label: Clorox says the sodium hypochlorite in its bleach products loses strength over time, roughly within a year. An old bottle that has sat under the sink for several years may not be doing much beyond adding a smell. If you are going to use bleach in a bathroom, use a reasonably fresh product, follow the dwell time on the label, rinse, and run the extractor fan while you work.

sections.h: Why Bleach Fails on Wood, Drywall and Other Porous Materials

blocks.p: Porous materials are full of tiny passages that absorb water: the fibres in wood, the paper facing and gypsum core of drywall, the pores of unsealed concrete and block, the backing of carpet. Mold grows into those passages. When you spray a bleach solution onto the face of the material, the explanation remediators usually give is that the chlorine reacts and is used up at or near the surface, where it meets the stain and other organic matter, while the water in the solution keeps soaking in. Household bleach is mostly water, so you are adding moisture to the very material the mold needs moisture to grow in.

The visible result is misleading. The surface pigment is oxidised and the stain disappears, so the wall or board looks clean. Underneath, growth that the chlorine did not reach is untouched, and the material is now damper than it was. That combination is why so many people report that mold came back in the same spot after a bleach treatment. It did not really come back. Most of it never left.

Bleach also brings its own damage. It can corrode metal fasteners and brackets, weaken some materials with repeated use, and permanently discolour wood and paint. Clorox's own directions rule out wood and painted surfaces for its Tilex spray for exactly these reasons. Even if bleach did reach every filament inside a stud, you would be trading a mold problem for a bleached, wet and possibly weakened stud.

On structural wood, such as joists, studs, subfloor and roof sheathing, the usual approach is to scrub or wire-brush the surface growth, vacuum it with a HEPA vacuum, apply a registered fungicide that is labelled for porous surfaces and keep it wet for its full contact time, then dry the wood thoroughly. Growth that remains in the grain can be sanded out, and permanent staining can be sealed with a stain-blocking primer. Wood that is soft or crumbling from rot needs replacing, not treating.

Drywall is the worst case for bleach. The paper facing is food for mold, the gypsum core absorbs water, and both are damaged by soaking. EPA guidance on porous materials is blunt: absorbent materials that become moldy, such as ceiling tiles and carpet, may have to be thrown away, because the mold can grow into the empty spaces and crevices and may be impossible to remove completely. Small surface spots on painted drywall can be cleaned and treated, but drywall that is soft, stained through or growing on the back should be cut out and replaced, and the wall cavity dried before new board goes up.

sections.h: What the EPA Actually Says About Bleach and Mold

blocks.p: The EPA's position is the one most guidance traces back to. In its mold cleanup guidance, including the "Should I use bleach to clean up mold?" page and its mold remediation guide, the EPA says the use of a chemical or biocide that kills organisms such as mold, with chlorine bleach as the example, is not recommended as a routine practice during mold cleanup. It adds that there may be instances when professional judgment indicates its use, for example when immune-compromised people are present.

The reasoning matters more than the rule. The EPA points out that it is usually neither possible nor desirable to sterilise an area, because a background level of mold spores will always remain, and those spores will not grow if the moisture problem has been fixed. It also notes that dead mold can still cause allergic reactions in some people, so it is not enough to kill mold. It must be removed. A bleached patch of dead mold still left on a wall has not solved the problem.

For hard surfaces, the EPA's basic advice is to scrub mold off with detergent and water and dry the area completely. If you do decide to use a disinfectant or biocide, it says to ventilate the area, exhaust the air to the outdoors, and never mix chlorine bleach with cleaning products that contain ammonia, because toxic fumes could be produced. The CDC's cleanup advice after floods is consistent: if you use bleach, use no more than 1 cup of household bleach in 1 gallon of water, never use it undiluted, and never mix it with ammonia or other cleaners.

OSHA's archived flood-cleanup guidance takes a similar line for workers, listing bleach as an optional disinfectant only after cleaning with detergent and water, mainly because floodwater can carry sewage. That is a sanitation step for contaminated surfaces, not an endorsement of bleach as the way to kill mold growing inside walls. Across all three agencies the message is the same: clean, dry and fix the moisture first, and treat disinfection as optional and secondary.

The EPA also gives a size threshold. If the moldy area is larger than about 10 square feet, roughly a 3-by-3-foot patch, it suggests following its larger-scale remediation guidance, and many homeowners will want a professional at that point. Mold that keeps returning, mold in an HVAC system, or mold after contaminated flooding are also cases where a pro is worth the call. Our guide to [crawl space mold removal](/crawl-space-mold-removal/) covers one of the most common places those larger jobs turn up.

blocks.p: Two patterns stand out. First, bleach is only the right answer in the top rows, where the material is smooth and sealed. Second, on almost every porous surface the recommendation is the same product, RMR-141, because it is an EPA-registered fungicide whose maker lists porous as well as non-porous surfaces, and it does not whiten or corrode the way bleach does. Its registration number is 61178-2-93443, and it uses two quaternary ammonium compounds at 0.07 percent each rather than chlorine.

Concrete and block deserve a word. Bleach will lighten surface mold on a basement wall, but unsealed masonry is porous and the mold is usually there because water is wicking through it. Clean and treat the growth, then deal with the water: grading, gutters, a [basement wall sealer](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) for minor seepage, and humidity control for the air. Otherwise the wall will grow mold again whatever you sprayed on it.

sections.h: Bleach Safety: The Mistakes That Hurt People

blocks.p: If you do use bleach, the biggest danger is not the mold. It is what bleach does when it meets other cleaners. Mixing bleach with ammonia, which is found in some glass cleaners and multi-surface sprays, produces chloramine gas. Mixing it with acids, which include vinegar, many toilet bowl cleaners and rust removers, releases chlorine gas. Both can injure your lungs in a small, closed bathroom. Clorox's own label warns against mixing its product with toilet bowl cleaners, rust removers, acids or ammonia.

This matters especially for mold, because people often try one product, see the stain return, and reach for another. Someone who sprays vinegar on a patch of mildew and follows it with bleach an hour later can create exactly the reaction the label warns about. If you switch products, rinse the surface with plain water and let it dry first. Our guide to whether [vinegar kills mold](/does-vinegar-kill-mold/) explains where vinegar fits and why the two must never meet.

Ventilation is the next rule. Open a window, run the bathroom fan, and take breaks if the smell builds up. The EPA says to exhaust the air to the outdoors whenever you use a disinfectant or biocide. Wear rubber or nitrile gloves and eye protection, because a splash of bleach in the eye is a trip to urgent care, and protect clothing and nearby fabric. For stain removers like RMR-86, which the safety data sheet lists at 1 to 5 percent sodium hypochlorite, RMR recommends a respirator with appropriate cartridges, protective clothing and nitrile gloves.

Finally, do not use bleach undiluted on mold in the house, and do not use more than the label calls for. Stronger does not mean better on a porous surface, because the problem is reach, not strength. If you are dealing with a large area, mold you can smell but not find, or someone in the house with asthma or a weakened immune system, the EPA's advice to consider a professional applies before you open any bottle.
NEVER MIX
Bleach plus ammonia, or bleach plus vinegar or other acids, makes toxic gas.
Rinse and dry between products. Ventilate. Wear gloves and eye protection. Never use bleach undiluted on household mold.

sections.h: What to Use Instead, and How to Keep Mold From Coming Back

blocks.p: For shower grout, tile and tubs, keep using a bleach spray if you like it. Clorox Plus Tilex is the right tool there and the one most people already own. Spray, let it work, rinse, and dry the surfaces afterwards with a squeegee or towel. If you would rather avoid chlorine fumes in a small bathroom, a registered non-bleach fungicide also works on those surfaces, it just will not remove staining as quickly.

For wood, drywall, concrete and other porous surfaces, use a registered fungicide labelled for them. RMR-141 is our pick. The label directions for mold are to saturate the surface and keep it wet for 10 minutes, then wipe or let it air dry. That 10-minute wet contact is what the kill claim depends on, so on a vertical wall you may need to re-spray to keep it wet. Spraying and wiping immediately does not deliver what the label promises. Our [RMR-141 review](/rmr-141-review/) goes through the label, the safety data sheet and where it fits in more detail.

Then deal with the stain separately, if it bothers you. Killing mold does not remove the dark marks it leaves, and RMR-141 does not remove stains. RMR-86 is the stain step. It is worth knowing why it works so fast: RMR-86 is itself bleach-based, and RMR's own FAQ says it does not kill mold, it only removes the stains. That is the same split this whole page describes. Kill with a registered fungicide, then whiten with bleach if you need to, on surfaces bleach will not damage. On wood or drywall where you do not want bleach, sand or seal the stain with a stain-blocking primer instead.

None of these products stops mold returning if the surface stays damp. EPA guidance is to dry water-damaged materials within 24 to 48 hours to prevent mold growth, and to keep indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent. Fix leaks, vent bathrooms and dryers outdoors, and watch for condensation on cold walls and windows. A cheap hygrometer tells you quickly whether a room is in range.

In basements, laundry rooms and other spaces that sit above 60 percent for weeks at a time, a dehumidifier is the tool that actually keeps mold away. For most rooms a 50-pint unit is the sensible size, and our guide to the [best 50-pint dehumidifier](/best-50-pint-dehumidifier/) covers the models worth buying, including Wi-Fi units that let you set the target humidity and check it from your phone. For larger or wetter basements, see our [basement dehumidifier guide](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/). If the room already stays between 30 and 50 percent, you do not need one, and money is better spent on fixing the leak.

Put together, the routine is simple. Find and fix the water. Remove what is too far gone. Scrub what can be saved, treat porous surfaces with RMR-141 for the full 10 minutes, use bleach only on hard bathroom surfaces, deal with stains last, and keep the humidity down so the problem does not start again. For the full product comparison, see our [best mold remover](/best-mold-remover/) picks.

mistakes: A stain that disappears in seconds proves the bleach reached the pigment, not that the colony is dead. On porous materials growth can remain inside the material. Judge the job by whether mold returns over the next few weeks, and by whether you have fixed the moisture that let it grow in the first place.
Spraying bleach on drywall or wood

Clorox itself says not to use its Tilex spray on wood or painted surfaces. On drywall and bare wood bleach adds water to the material, discolours it and does not reliably reach growth inside. Use a registered fungicide labelled for porous surfaces, and replace drywall that is soft or stained through.

Mixing bleach with acids such as vinegar releases chlorine gas, and mixing it with ammonia releases chloramine. Both can happen on the surface if you switch products without rinsing. Rinse with plain water and let the area dry between products, ventilate the room, and never combine cleaners in a bucket.

A fungicide kill claim depends on the surface staying wet for the time on the label. RMR-141 needs 10 minutes of wet contact for mold. Spraying and wiping straight away, or letting a vertical wall dry in two minutes, means the label claim does not apply. Re-spray to keep it wet.
Treating mold but not the moisture

Every product on this page is a second line of defence. Mold returns wherever a surface stays damp, so fix leaks, dry wet materials within 24 to 48 hours as EPA guidance advises, and keep humidity below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50, with ventilation or a dehumidifier.
bottomLine: Bleach kills mold where mold cannot hide: glazed tile, glass, tubs and sealed surfaces. Keep it for the shower. On wood, drywall, concrete and anything else that soaks up water, it removes the stain and leaves the problem, which is why the EPA does not recommend it as a routine part of mold cleanup. For porous surfaces, use a registered fungicide such as RMR-141 and keep it wet for the full 10 minutes, then remove stains separately if you need to. And fix the moisture, because a room held between 30 and 50 percent humidity is the only mold treatment that keeps working after you put the bottle away.

faqs.a: On hard, non-porous surfaces such as glazed tile, glass, tubs and sealed counters, yes. Bleach kills surface mold and removes the stain. On porous materials such as wood, drywall and concrete it mostly whitens the stain while growth inside the material remains. The EPA does not recommend bleach as a routine part of mold cleanup; detergent, water and drying come first.

faqs.q: Will bleach kill mold on wood?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Wood is porous, so mold grows into the grain where a bleach spray does not dependably reach, and the water in the solution soaks in. Bleach also discolours wood, and Clorox says not to use its Tilex spray on wood. Scrub, apply a registered fungicide such as RMR-141 for its full 10-minute contact time, then dry it completely.

Black mold is a colour, not a separate kind of mold that responds differently. On non-porous surfaces bleach kills dark mold as well as any other. On porous ones it bleaches the black colour out and leaves growth underneath. If black mold covers more than about 10 square feet, EPA guidance suggests a larger-scale approach, often a professional.

faqs.q: Does bleach kill black mold on drywall?
faqs.a: No, not dependably. Drywall paper and gypsum absorb water and mold grows into them, so bleach removes the surface stain without reaching growth inside, and the soaking can damage the board. Small surface spots on painted drywall can be cleaned and treated with a registered fungicide. Drywall that is soft or stained through should be cut out and replaced.

faqs.q: Why does mold come back after bleach?
faqs.a: Usually because it never left. Bleach removed the visible stain while the colony inside a porous material survived, or the moisture that fed it was never fixed. Mold also returns on any surface that stays damp. Fix the water source, treat porous surfaces with a registered fungicide, and keep indoor humidity between 30 and 50 percent.

faqs.q: What kills mold better than bleach?
faqs.a: On porous surfaces, an EPA-registered fungicide labelled for them, such as RMR-141, a quaternary ammonium product that requires 10 minutes of wet contact for mold and does not whiten. On shower tile and grout, a bleach spray like Clorox Plus Tilex works well. Vinegar is not a registered mold killer. Whatever you use, removing the mold and fixing moisture matter most.

faqs.q: Is it safe to mix bleach with other cleaners for mold?
faqs.a: No. Bleach with ammonia produces chloramine gas, and bleach with acids such as vinegar, toilet bowl cleaner or rust remover releases chlorine gas. Use one product at a time, rinse with water and let the surface dry before switching, ventilate the room, and wear gloves and eye protection. The CDC says never to use bleach undiluted.
